<meta>continues from previous page</meta>all the organs and instruments are clearly present, by means of which these same movements could also be carried out in a machine. This is so much the case that even in ourselves, the mind does not move the external limbs directly. Instead, it only directs the spirits <note>original: *spiritus*; referring to "animal spirits," which 17th-century physiology considered a subtle fluid responsible for nerve transmission.</note> flowing from the heart through the brain into the muscles, and determines them toward certain movements; for these spirits are, of their own accord, applied just as easily to many different actions.

Indeed, most of the movements that occur within us do not depend on the mind at all. Such are the beating of the heart, the digestion of food, nutrition, the breathing of those who sleep, and even in those who are awake, walking, singing, and similar activities when they occur without the mind paying attention to them.

And when those who fall from a height reach their hands out before them to protect the head, they certainly do this by no counsel of reason, but only because the sight of the impending fall, reaching as far as the brain, sends the animal spirits into the nerves in the manner necessary to produce this movement, even against the will of the mind, and just as if in a machine.

And since this is held for certain in our own case...

<summary>Descartes explains that many human bodily functions are purely mechanical and occur without conscious thought, comparing the body to a machine directed by animal spirits. He uses reflexes, like catching oneself during a fall, to demonstrate that the body can act independently of the mind's will.</summary>
<keywords>animal spirits, physiology, reflexes, machine, mind-body interaction, brain, heart, involuntary movement</keywords>
